s is a web app (per prompt), so "native-feeling" means fast, mobile-first web: large tap targets on the offer form, legible and fast-loading on a phone first, no desktop-only interaction patterns. A slow or broken mobile load is the single most likely failure mode when this gets shared, since most first visits will come from a phone.

**Major assumptions and risks:**
1. Traffic is single-session and spiky, not habitual — ASSUMPTION, shapes the priority toward fast comprehension over retention features.
2. Moderation risk is high: anonymous submissions + public leaderboard + content about a child is an abuse magnet (slurs, harassment, impersonation). A basic content filter (blocklist/length check) at submission time should be part of MVP form validation, not deferred to post-hoc reporting alone.
3. The offers/leaderboard screen is the highest-risk layout for the no-overlapping-text rule — long names, large dollar figures, and timestamps need explicit collision handling, tested with adversarial-length content, not just happy-path data.
4. Tone/reputational risk: airtight disclaimers can still get cropped out of a shared screenshot. The non-binding "this is just for fun, parents decide" framing should live in the homepage headline/hero copy itself, not only as a pre-submission footnote — reinforces DEC-prompt_contract-001 rather than adding new scope.

**Implications for the first build:** Ship the single personal listing (the contracted MVP) extremely well: a populated hero with the disclaimer woven into the headline copy, a working offer form with real validation plus a lightweight content filter, a sorted public offers list stress-tested against long names/large numbers/long aliases colliding, demo-labeled checkout, and report/flag controls on the listing and every offer. If the multi-user marketplace stretch goal has to be cut to protect this quality bar, that must be stated explicitly per DEC-prompt_contract-002 — a single polished listing beats a marketplace with a visibly half-done create-flow or browse page.

Dense reference for building correct, accessible, maintainable web UI in 2026. Examples use React/JSX + TypeScript, but the rules generalize. Every snippet is idiomatic and compiles.

## Component Structure

### Rules
- **One component, one responsibility.** If a component both fetches data and renders complex layout, split it (container/presentational, or hook + view).
- **Colocate** the component, its styles, tests, and stories in one folder: `Button/{Button.tsx, Button.module.css, Button.test.tsx}`.
- **Props over prop-drilling.** Reach for context only for cross-cutting concerns (theme, auth, locale, router), not to avoid passing 2 props.
- **Composition over boolean explosion.** Don't accumulate `isPrimary`, `isLarge`, `hasIcon`. Use `variant`/`size` union types and slot children.
- **Controlled where the parent needs the value; uncontrolled otherwise.** Don't mirror props into state — derive during render.
- **Render the correct element.** A thing that navigates is `<a>`; a thing that acts is `<button>`. Never `<div onClick>`.
- **Stable keys.** Use domain IDs as list keys, never array index for reorderable/filterable lists.

### Composable, typed component (variant pattern)
In React 19, `ref` is a regular prop — `forwardRef` is no longer required for new code (and is deprecated). Type `ref` directly.
```tsx
import type { ButtonHTMLAttributes, Ref } from 'react';
import clsx from 'clsx';
import styles from './Button.module.css';

type ButtonProps = ButtonHTMLAttributes<HTMLButtonElement> & {
  variant?: 'primary' | 'secondary' | 'ghost';
  size?: 'sm' | 'md' | 'lg';
  ref?: Ref<HTMLButtonElement>;
};

export function Button({
  variant = 'primary',
  size = 'md',
  className,
  type = 'button',
  ...props
}: ButtonProps) {
  return (
    <button
      type={type}
      className={clsx(styles.button, styles[variant], styles[size], className)}
      {...props}
    />
  );
}
```
- Exposing `ref` lets parents focus/measure the node (essential for menus, tooltips, form libs).
- Default `type="button"` so a button inside a `<form>` doesn't accidentally submit; consumers can still override.
- Spread `...props` after your defaults so consumers can pass `aria-*`, `onClick`, `disabled`.
- Allow `className` passthrough for one-off overrides without new variants.

> On React ≤18 (or libraries needing it), wrap with `forwardRef<HTMLButtonElement, ButtonProps>(...)` instead of a `ref` prop.

### Slots / compound components
Assign sub-components with `Object.assign` so TypeScript sees them as properties of the parent (bare `Card.Header = ...` errors under `strict`).
```tsx
import type { ReactNode } from 'react';

function CardRoot({ children }: { children: ReactNode }) {
  return <section className={styles.card}>{children}</section>;
}
function CardHeader({ children }: { children: ReactNode }) {
  return <header className={styles.cardHeader}>{children}</header>;
}
function CardBody({ children }: { children: ReactNode }) {
  return <div className={styles.cardBody}>{children}</div>;
}

export const Card = Object.assign(CardRoot, { Header: CardHeader, Body: CardBody });
// <Card><Card.Header>…</Card.Header><Card.Body>…</Card.Body></Card>
```
Compound components give consumers layout freedom without a prop for every slot.

### Anti-patterns
- Passing JSX through props (`title={<Icon/>}`) when `children` or a slot would do.
- `useEffect` to sync derived state — compute it in render or with `useMemo`.
- Giant `index.ts` barrels that break tree-shaking and create circular imports.
- Components that read `window`/`document` during render (breaks SSR/hydration). Guard with `useEffect`, `useSyncExternalStore`, or `typeof window !== 'undefined'`.

## Styling: Tailwind CSS v4

Tailwind v4 is **CSS-first**: no `tailwind.config.js` by default. You import Tailwind and declare tokens in CSS with `@theme`. The engine (Oxide) is dramatically faster; browser targets are modern (uses `@property`, cascade layers, `color-mix()`).

### Setup
```css
/* app.css */
@import "tailwindcss";

@theme {
  --color-brand-50:  oklch(0.97 0.02 265);
  --color-brand-500: oklch(0.62 0.19 265);
  --color-brand-600: oklch(0.55 0.20 265);
  --font-sans: "Inter var", system-ui, sans-serif;
  --radius-card: 0.75rem;
  --breakpoint-3xl: 120rem;        /* adds 3xl: variant */

```

- `--font-*` → `font-sans`; `--radius-*` → `rounded-card`; `--breakpoint-*` → new responsive variants.
- The spacing scale is derived from a built-in `--spacing` base (`0.25rem`), so `p-4` = `1rem` out of the box; override `--spacing` in `@theme` only if you need a different unit.
- Tokens are emitted as real CSS variables at `:root`, so third-party/custom CSS can read `var(--color-brand-500)` and you can inspect them in DevTools.

### Utility-first rules
- **Compose utilities inline; don't prematurely extract.** Repetition in markup is cheaper than a leaky abstraction. Extract into a component when the *markup* repeats, not just the classes.

Eleven-plus rounds of "npm install is blocked," a backend that was never built, and a QA script written against that is worth something, but only if it's honest that step one of the actual checklist is "does npm install even complete" — because nobody in this project's history has verified that, and if it fails, every single downstream step is moot. I'm going to write the script assuming someone finally gets a working `npm install && npm run dev`, but I'll flag every place where the checklist itself is testing against known-missing functionality rather than pretending it'll pass.

Cold load, first thing a real visitor sees: open the root URL on a phone-width viewport, throttled to slow 4G if the device supports it. Expected: the hero, headline with the baked-in non-binding disclaimer, story block, and the empty-state leaderboard render immediately in the initial HTML — no spinner-then-content flash, no layout shift when the leaderboard mounts. This is the R-001/design_handoff-007 SSR requirement; if you see a blank screen for even a frame before content appears, that's a hard fail, not a nitpick, because this fleet has shipped that exact failure before. Confirm the empty leaderboard shows the designed icon+copy+CTA, not "no data" or a bare list. Tap the CTA and confirm it scrolls to or focuses the offer form — a CTA that does nothing on tap is worse than no CTA.

Offer submission, happy path: tap "make an offer," confirm the sheet opens with focus trapped inside it (tab through every field, confirm focus never escapes to the page behind, confirm the sheet's own close button gets focus and Escape closes it and returns focus to the trigger button). Fill alias, story, amount with normal values. Confirm inline validation reacts as you type, not only on submit. Submit and confirm you're taken through the disclaimer step before checkout — the disclaimer must be its own visible acknowledgment, not something you can breeze past by tapping the same button twice. Confirm the demo checkout sheet shows a static, non-editable "card" — try to tap into the card number field and confirm nothing happens; there should be no cursor, no focus ring, no way to type a real card number into anything on this screen. Tap demo-pay and watch for the receipt-flip animation and the leaderboard reorder. This is the single most important moment in the whole app per five separate phase decisions, so don't just glance at it — confirm your own card visibly glows/pulses in its new slot, confirm the rank number is correct, and confirm a screen reader (VoiceOver/TalkBack, or at minimum inspect the aria-live region in devtools) actually announces the new rank. If you only check this visually, you've verified half the requirement.

Content filter: submit something from the shared blocked-word fixture (not something you invent yourself — use the actual file both the filter and the flow are supposed to share) and confirm you get a specific, actionable rejection reason, not a generic "invalid submission." Then submit a legitimate non-English name with an apostrophe or diacritic (e.g. "D'Angelo" or "Renée") and confirm it's accepted — this is the false-positive case three phases worried about, and it's exactly the kind of thing that looks fine in code review and breaks in practice.

Failure path — this is the one I'd bet money nobody has actually watched happen: submit an offer, let the checkout animation start, then kill your network connection mid-submission (airplane mode, or throttle to offline in devtools) before it resolves. The spec is explicit that the success/reorder spectacle must never complete and then reveal failure afterward — confirm you get a distinct failure state with a retry action, your form data is preserved (you shouldn't have to retype everything), and no "offer confirmed" copy ever appeared before the failure showed. If the UI shows success and then silently fails, or shows success and then just leaves you there, that's the worst possible failure mode for this product's core promise and it needs to be called out as a blocker, not a known gap.

But here's my real skepticism: as of the last verification round, there is no backend anywhere in this repo. No database, no `/api/offers`. That means the "happy path" I just described above literally cannot be observed — every real submission attempt, against actual running code, will hit the failure branch, every time, because there's nothing on the other end to say yes. So the QA checklist has to be honest about this: the failure-and-retry path is the only path that can currently be manually verified end to end, and it should be tested first, not last, because it's the only thing that's real right now. Anyone running this checklist needs to know they will not see a successful checkout complete until the backend exists — that's not a QA failure, that's the state of the product, and the checklist should say so explicitly rather than have a tester assume they did something wrong.

Report/flag: on the listing itself and on an individual offer card, tap report, confirm instant confirmation copy, confirm the button becomes disabled/labeled "reported" and can't be tapped again from the same device. Then clear localStorage (devtools > Application > Clear storage, simulating what Safari ITP does on its own after about a week) and confirm the item becomes reportable again — this was flagged as a real, distinct edge case from "storage never available," and it should be tested as its own step, not assumed covered by a generic storage test. Separately, confirm three reports on the same offer (from three different simulated devices/incognito windows, since one device can only report once) actually hides it from the public list, and confirm it's a soft-hide — if you have any way to inspect the data layer, confirm the row still exists rather than being deleted.

Rate limit: submit five offers back to back, then try a sixth within the ten-minute window, confirm you're blocked with a message that tells you when you can try again, and confirm it's not a permanent lock — legitimate repeat joke offers need to eventually get through.

Leaderboard stress test, the highest-risk screen per this project's own history: use the dev seed toggle (if it ships to a real build — if it doesn't, this step is untestable and that itself is worth flagging) to load the adversarial fixture: the 60-character alias, the $9,999,999 offer, and the three tied-amount offers. At 360px and 390px width, in both light and dark mode, confirm nothing overlaps — the long alias doesn't collide with the amount, the amount doesn't collide with the rank badge, and the three tied offers render as three distinct rows with a stable, non-flickering order rather than jumping around on every refresh. Do this specific check twice, once right after page load and once after triggering a reorder animation, since a collision that only appears mid-animation is exactly the kind of bug a static screenshot review misses.

Dark mode and light mode: toggle OS-level appearance mid-session (not just on load) and confirm the page actually re-themes live, since there's no persisted user toggle to fall back on — this was called out as load-bearing behavior, not a nice-to-have. Check contrast specifically on dollar amounts and body text against both pastel-adjacent backgrounds; don't just eyeball it, use a contrast checker on at least the price text in both modes.

Accessibility beyond the aria-live check above: tab through the entire home page in order and confirm the tab order matches visual order, confirm every interactive element has a visible focus ring, confirm both sheets return focus to their trigger on close, confirm every checkout field — even the decorative ones — has a real accessible label so a screen-reader user understands this is an intentional fake rather than a broken form, and confirm images/icons that are purely decorative (the empty-state icon, emoji) are marked `aria-hidden`.

Persistence and offline: there's no offline queue in this build (explicitly deferred), so the correct behavior when offline is a clear error, not a silent hang or a fake-success. Test it: go offline, try to submit, confirm you get an honest "you're offline" or network-failure message rather than the app pretending to work.

Subscription/paywall: there isn't one — the Patron pass was deferred out of this build entirely, so there's nothing to test here, and the checklist should say that plainly rather than leave a blank paywall section that looks like an oversight.

Regression check across all of this: after any successful (or, right now, any failed-and-retried) submission, refresh the page and confirm the leaderboard state is what you'd expect — for the currently-real failure path, that means confirming a failed offer did NOT appear in the list after refresh, since a phantom entry from a failed write would be a worse bug than the failure itself.

The thing I most want preserved in the final output: a QA checklist that pretends this app currently completes a real transaction would be a form of the exact "claims an outcome that hasn't happened" violation this whole project has been careful to avoid everywhere else. The honest version of this checklist tests the failure/retry path as the primary currently-verifiable flow, documents the happy path as "cannot be observed until the backend exists, here is what it should look like when it can," and doesn't let anyone mistake a thoroughly-read codebase for a working one.
